findings.text: A newcomer learns what Athena is in the first sentence, and the second sentence gives a concrete reason to care: one model does the work and a different one checks it, and each step's cost is recorded.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: On Athena's own site, the title and nearly all of the page are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to read three header paragraphs to see that the firstmate material is a demonstration and not the product.
findings.source: Page title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page describes Athena as a tool that changes code, but what it shows off is a study, which is a reading task. It never explains how studies relate to requests, or how to produce one. A reader impressed by the study is given only a command for a code change.
findings.source: Lede: "turns a short request into a change to a code repository" vs. "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project"; Next steps: "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The next step is easy to find: the header links to it, and that section gives the repository link, an install command and a first command to try.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The install step assumes you already have a checkout. It gives no clone command and names no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or the AI model access that the lede implies is needed.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: Each statement can be checked: claim ids link to exact file lines at a pinned commit. This shows Athena's main selling point in action rather than just stating it.
findings.source: Header lede: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it"; Claims and sources entries link to e.g. "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197"

findings.text: The firstmate sections go deep into exit codes, pending-close records and secondmates. That suits someone evaluating firstmate, but it is much more than a newcomer to Athena needs. The "Start here" section and the glossary help, but the depth hides the page's main message.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75 ... lock contention or an unreadable capacity declaration refuses with exit 1"

findings.text: The limits section exposes the study's internal process ("a first reading missed") and uses the tags "not run" and "read". A newcomer cannot easily turn these into a sense of how far to trust the page.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths: ... They are read from the pinned source and none was run"

findings.text: The `studies/` folder is not linked and its repository is not named, so a newcomer cannot follow this pointer.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
